title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Residents push to recall a supervisor amid fights over power, water and local control.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy. Tonight we're diving into how one township's recall effort is shining a light on the bigger battles over these massive projects.

That's right, Emmy. The big story today comes out of Springfield Township in Oakland County, where residents are gathering signatures to recall the supervisor they say fast-tracked data center approvals that could overload roads, power and water.
Graham, why is this recall effort landing now? What's the history here with data centers in these southeast Michigan townships?

Well, these fights have been building for months. Springfield itself put a temporary moratorium in place earlier this year after officials realized the township wasn't prepared for the impacts. Similar stories have played out in places like Saline and Lyon, where residents pushed back hard against hyperscale projects.
And now it's turning into recall campaigns. How many of these efforts are we seeing statewide?

Reports show dozens of recall pushes tied directly to data center disputes this year. It's reshaping local politics because voters are holding officials accountable for decisions that could change their communities for good.
What exactly are residents worried about with these facilities? The power side seems huge.

It is. A single large data center can demand hundreds of megawatts or more — think the output of a nuclear plant in some cases. Utilities like DTE and Consumers Energy have announced deals for gigawatts of new load, which could mean higher rates for everyone if infrastructure costs get passed along.
And water use? I've heard these places need millions of gallons a day for cooling.

Exactly. We're talking one to five million gallons daily per big facility in some estimates. That draws from aquifers or municipal systems and raises concerns about wells running low, especially in rural spots without big treatment plants.
Farmland is another piece, right? These projects often go on open land.
Yes, and that shifts tax bases and land use. A successful recall in Springfield could flip control of future approvals, giving residents more say in zoning and whether projects move forward at all.
So what happens next with the signature drive? How long could this drag on?
Petitions are circulating now. If they gather enough valid signatures, it heads to a vote that could remove the supervisor and change the board's direction on these deals.
This feels like it's spreading. How does it connect to all the moratoriums popping up?
Over 50 communities have paused new applications to study the rules. It's a way to buy time without an outright ban, which state law makes tricky.
Got it. So the recall is really a symptom of this statewide tension over who decides where these power-hungry projects land.
Precisely. And listeners 30 or 60 miles away could feel it in their electric bills or local grid reliability if big approvals keep coming.
Thanks for grounding that, Graham. Let's move to some quick hits from the past couple days.
Starting with Ypsilanti. The city council extended its data center moratorium today while it studies power and water impacts. That pause blocks large projects for now.
And ripple effects could reach Ann Arbor and beyond on electricity rates if things move later. Smart move to get more data first.
Yesterday a developer restarted plans to turn an old electric plant site into a data center. Tax revenue questions are front and center there.
Residents nearby will watch how that affects land use and rates. Meanwhile, Mason County broke ground on two major facilities yesterday — construction jobs but big draws on the regional grid.
Kalamazoo added a moratorium to its zoning code on Saturday to slow the rush as AI proposals multiply. Gives time to study noise, power and water.
Garfield Township in Grand Traverse County is taking a full year to draft its own rules, announced Friday. That delay lets locals weigh traffic, taxes and grid impacts.
Also Friday, a university town hall gave Mid-Michigan residents their first concrete look at megawatt and water demands from proposed centers.
Lakeshore Township blocked projects using existing zoning on Friday, keeping water and noise concerns off the table for now. Nearby towns are taking notes.
And Ypsilanti-area residents planned a protest Friday over water use at two proposed campuses that could pull millions of gallons daily.
Finally, a farm is seeking city annexation to build on rural land, which would shift taxes and control away from the township.
Now for on deck — what listeners can actually attend or follow.
Garfield Township supervisors will spend the next 12 months crafting standards, so keep an eye on their public meetings for input on noise, power and water limits.
The Mid-Michigan town hall series is ongoing, with more sessions planned where residents within 30 miles can question developers on rates and aquifers.
Springfield's recall process itself will have public steps — signature verification and potential hearings worth watching if you're in Oakland County.
And Kalamazoo's new zoning work will likely include hearings soon as they formalize the moratorium.
Plenty happening locally. Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Springfield Recall Sparks Fresh Look at Data Center Strain Across Michigan
